# leakguard

**One detection engine, two hosts.** Secret-exposure seatbelt for AI coding
agents: it stops the agent reading credentials, redacts them from tool output, and
blocks a credential from leaving the machine.

Detection is delegated to [**betterleaks**](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks),
a single static binary with 471 rules. This project is the layer a scanner cannot
be: *may the agent read this file*, *is this command exporting it*, *what should
the model be told when the gate refuses*.

| host | package | install |
|---|---|---|
| [pi.dev](https://pi.dev) | `pi-leakguard` (repo root) | `pi install git:github.com/calionauta/leakguard` |
| [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) | `oc-leakguard` (`packages/oc-leakguard/`) | `opencode plugin add github:calionauta/leakguard` or `scripts/install-oc.sh` |

**Neither needs an npm publish.** Both resolve a GitHub repo directly: `pi`
installs from the repository root, OpenCode accepts a Git package specifier.

Installing once is not the same as staying installed. Both hosts can be *correct on
disk and broken in practice*, in ways that never surface as an error: `pi` does not
pull its git checkout, and a long-running `opencode serve` keeps the module it
loaded in memory and reports `Plugin failed` after the files change underneath it.
`scripts/check-installs.sh` checks every surface, including whether the running
process actually loaded the current code.

Shared in `core/`: the engine client, the blocked-path rules, and the egress
judgement. Per host, only the hook API and the wording of a refusal. That split is
deliberate -- when these were two copies, the same egress blind spot existed in
both at once and had to be fixed twice.

> **Note:** an independent continuation of `@raquezha/noleaks`' ideas, not an
> official fork. MIT licence, attribution kept.

> **Security model:** a powerful defense-in-depth "seatbelt", **not** an airtight
> sandbox. It stops accidental leaks and common exfiltration patterns. For
> untrusted code or unattended automation, use a real sandbox (Docker, Micro-VM).

## Install

### 1. The engine (required)

```sh
~/.bin/betterleaks-update          # installs betterleaks, checksum-verified
```

Nothing works without it except the path guards. The pi extension asks once at
install time; the OpenCode plugin and the git hook report DEGRADED and name the
command. Updates are **reported, never applied** -- the rules are compiled into
the binary, so a version bump is a rule change and must be reviewed.

### 2. pi.dev

```sh
pi install git:github.com/calionauta/leakguard
```

### 3. OpenCode

```sh
opencode plugin add github:calionauta/leakguard   # installs a pinned snapshot
# or, from a checkout -- tracks the checkout and verifies what it wrote:
scripts/install-oc.sh
```

`install-oc.sh` is preferred when you work on this repo, because it re-checks the
copied files and cleans up the legacy single-file plugin. Either way, **restart
OpenCode afterwards**: the plugin is cached per process, so correcting the files
does not affect a running `opencode serve`.

### 4. The commit gate (optional, recommended)

```sh
cp hooks/pre-commit ~/.git-hooks/pre-commit && chmod +x ~/.git-hooks/pre-commit
git config --global core.hooksPath ~/.git-hooks
```

### Verify, rather than assume

```sh
python3 scripts/verify-engine.py     # engine rules intact, no local override
scripts/check-installs.sh --remote   # every host surface, both machines
npm test                             # 151 unit tests
npm run typecheck                    # root extension AND the OpenCode host
```

## Security model & limitations

When a layer fires, here's what happens:

- **BLOCK** — leakguard stops the tool call (unless you allow it via the confirm prompt or `/leakguard mode auto`).
- **REDACT** — leakguard replaces the secret text with `[LEAKGUARD_REDACTED]` before the model sees it; the agent still knows a secret *exists*, just not its value.
- **WARN** — leakguard shows a notification; it doesn't block anything.

| Layer | Action | What it catches | False-positive risk | False-negative risk |
| ----- | ------ | --------------- | ------------------ | ------------------ |
| Path protection (read/write/delete) | BLOCK (confirm) | Access to `.env`, `~/.ssh`, `/etc/shadow`, etc. | Low — patterns are specific file names | Medium — custom secret paths need manual config |
| Secret redaction (output) | REDACT | anything the betterleaks engine reports (471 rules) plus two residual shapes | Low -- engine rules carry context, entropy and stopword filters | Medium -- a credential shape with no upstream rule |
| Symlink guard | BLOCK | Symlink bypass to a sensitive file | Very low | Low — `realpathSync` resolves before checking |
| Obfuscation (NFKC/control chars) | BLOCK | Homoglyph / zero-width bypass in commands | Low — normal whitespace is allowed | Low — only rejects clear variance |
| Shell exfil (env-dump, expansion, smuggle, discovery+secret) | BLOCK (confirm) | `env`, `$TOKEN`, `base64 \| curl`, `nmap`+secret | Low | Medium — arbitrarily obfuscated pipelines |
| Egress DLP | BLOCK (confirm) | `curl -u user:pass`, credentialed URLs, secret headers | Low — only fires on clear creds in egress | Medium — encoded/obfuscated payloads |
| Universal word scan | BLOCK (confirm) | `sudo chmod`, `dd`, `shred` as arguments | Low — only critical utils | Low | 
| Write/edit payload scan | BLOCK (confirm) | Secret material in write body | Low | Medium — novel formats |
| grep/find/ls guard | BLOCK (confirm) | These tools over sensitive paths | Low | Low |
| Taint tracking | BLOCK (confirm) | Egress of content read from a sensitive path | Low — only after a sensitive read | Medium — indirect leaks (e.g. summarizing then pasting) |
| Pre-commit/push scan | BLOCK (confirm) | Secret in `git diff` on commit/push | Low — scans diff, not whole tree | Medium — novel formats |
| Audit log | WARN (log only) | Every block/redact/allow event | None — observability | None |
| Extensible config | n/a | User allow/block paths + extra secret patterns | None — user-defined | None — user-defined |

### Why leakguard does not detect prompt injection by pattern

Detecting prompt injection with regex/heuristics is **not a consolidated
industry strategy**. Attackers write injections in endless variations
(obfuscation, other languages, indirect phrasing like "the previous
instructions are deprecated"), so a fixed pattern list misses almost everything
and false-positives on normal prose ("ignore the previous section"). Maintaining
that list costs more than it's worth.

So instead of trying to *catch* the injection, it stops the **harm** it causes:

- If the model gets tricked into reading a secret, **redaction** strips it
  from what it can see and repeat.
- If it gets tricked into exfiltrating, **egress DLP** and **taint
  tracking** block the network call carrying credentials.

Think of leakguard as shrinking the blast radius, not as a detector.

### Measured false positives (18 real repositories)

The blocking layer was measured against every tracked file in 18 repositories,
then the same files again after each fix:

| stage | files flagged | what was firing |
|---|---|---|
| before | **95** | `[0-9a-f]{32,}` matching `UPSTREAM_SHA` provenance, npm `integrity` digests, `sha256:` image pins |
| hex split into command/content layers | 21 | documentation and example configs |
| context-aware path allowlist | 2 | a `SK proj` placeholder, lowercase PEM inside a detector |
| placeholder list + case-sensitive `PEM_RE` | **0** | — |

Guarded by `coverage.test.ts`: every real credential shape (`ghp_`, `sk-`,
`sk-proj-`, `sk-ant-`, `AKIA`, `xoxb-`, PEM) must still be detected. A false
negative is worse than a false positive, so that test gates any rule change.

### How leakguard keeps false positives / false negatives in check

- **It confirms, it does not silently block.** Every BLOCK asks via `ctx.ui.confirm`
  (unless AUTO mode is active). This keeps the agent useful while still safe.
- **Conservative patterns.** leakguard's path and redaction patterns target specific
  file names and known secret prefixes; they avoid matching normal code.
- **AUTO mode** (🔥) provides the same protection as MAX but blocks silently
  without confirm prompts. Blocks are still recorded in stats and audit log.
  Redaction stays on. Persisted to `leakguard.json` like any other mode.
- **Redaction over blocking for output.** leakguard scrubs secrets from output
  instead of blocking it, which preserves agent utility (deploy still works via
  the environment) while preventing leakage — the preferred 2026 pattern of
  "don't give agents secrets".
- **Blocks that teach instead of just refusing.** Every block answers three
  questions in one line: **what matched** (the pattern name), **where** (tool,
  argument role, masked line number), and **what to do instead** (a remedy chosen
  for that pattern family). A block that says only "secret-looking material"
  leaves the model guessing, and guessing costs tokens on retries that cannot
  converge — see `llm-hints.ts`.
- **Repeat detection.** The second block of the same intent reads differently:
  "Changing the command's syntax will NOT change the outcome — the check is about
  the value, not the spelling. Stop retrying, or ask the human." The counter is
  per-turn, so a genuinely new task starts fresh.
- **Search-pattern recognition.** A sensitive token used as a *search pattern*
  (`grep -n 'DOTENV|\\.env' file.ts`) is not a file access. It is recognised as
  such and the block includes a copy-pasteable workaround instead of pushing the
  model toward reading whole files.
- **Documentation and fixtures are exempt.** `docs/`, `*.example.*`, `*.sample`,
  `*.template`, `testdata/`, test files, and vendored code may contain example
  credentials — that is what they are for. A real private key block is still
  caught anywhere.
- **`/leakguard describe` — shape, not value.** When a value is redacted, the
  model cannot tell a real leak from a false positive, so it either guesses or
  gives up on the file. Describe mode reports length, character classes, entropy
  bucket, a published vendor prefix, and whether the value looks like prose or a
  placeholder. Enough to classify the finding; nothing that helps an attacker.
  Unknown prefixes are never echoed.
- **Context note on redacted output.** Names the rules that fired, attaches to
  the block that actually changed, and on a repeat says plainly that re-running
  will not reveal the value.

## Features

- **Path protection**: leakguard blocks reads/writes/deletes of sensitive paths
  (`.env`, `~/.ssh/`, `~/.aws/`, `/etc/shadow`, Keychains, etc.)
- **Secret redaction**: leakguard scrubs API keys, tokens, passwords, private-key blocks,
  DB URLs, and secret assignments from `tool_result` content.
- **Informative placeholder**: redacted values show the pattern name that matched:
  `[LEAKGUARD_REDACTED — JWT Token]`. Helps the LLM understand what was redacted
  and ask for the right trust pattern.
- **Session trust**: mark a pattern as trusted for the current session. Leakguard
  skips redaction for output containing that pattern. LLM cannot self-bypass — only
  the human can run `/leakguard trust <pattern>`.
- **Symlink guard**: leakguard resolves paths to their *real* on-disk location before
  checking, so symlink bypasses are caught.
- **Obfuscation detection**: leakguard rejects NFKC normalization variance and hidden/control
  characters (homoglyph / zero-width attacks).
- **Shell exfiltration blocks**: leakguard blocks env dumps (`env`/`printenv`/`set`/`export`),
  sensitive variable expansion (`$TOKEN`), transform+smuggle (`base64`/`openssl`
  piping secrets), and discovery/exfil combine (`nmap`/`curl` + secrets).
- **Universal word scan**: leakguard blocks critical utilities even as nested arguments
  (`sudo chmod`, `dd`, `shred`, `mkfs`, ...).
- **Write/edit payload scan**: leakguard blocks writes whose body contains secret-looking
  material.
- **grep / find / ls guards**: leakguard blocks those tools over sensitive paths in
  `max` mode.
- **allow-once**: bypass redaction for one value without changing the mode.
  Human-only via confirm prompt — the LLM cannot trigger it.
- **Four modes** (persisted to `~/.pi/agent/leakguard.json`):
  - `max` — block sensitive paths AND redact secrets (with confirm prompts)
  - `auto` (default) — same as MAX, but blocks silently (no confirm prompts)
  - `basic` — allow reads but still redact secrets (Safe Debugging)
  - `off` — disable all protection (dangerous)

## What it blocks (in MAX mode)

| Category        | Examples                                                      |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Environment     | `.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.production`                       |
| Private keys    | `id_rsa`, `id_ed25519`, `*.pem`, `*.key`, `*.p12`, `*.keystore` |
| Credentials     | `auth.json`, `.npmrc`, `.netrc`, `.pypirc`, `.git-credentials` |
| Cloud config    | `~/.aws/`, `~/.azure/`, `~/.config/gcloud/`, `~/.docker/`, `~/.kube/` |
| SSH / GPG       | `~/.ssh/`, `~/.gnupg/`                                        |
| Pi secrets      | `.pi-secrets/`                                                |
| Shell config    | `.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, `.profile`                               |
| System          | `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers`, `/etc/passwd`                  |
| macOS Keychain  | `~/Library/Keychains/`                                        |

## What it redacts

Whatever the engine reports: AWS (key id, secret, session), OpenAI, Anthropic,
Google, GitHub (classic, fine-grained, OAuth, app, refresh), GitLab, Slack tokens
and webhooks, Stripe, SendGrid, npm, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler, 1Password (secret
key and service-account token), PEM private-key blocks, JWTs, database and
credential URLs, and key=/password= assignments -- 471 rules in total, plus the
two residual shapes listed below (Bearer headers without egress context, and
op:// references).

Because the engine ships 218 validators, a finding can also be reported as
valid, revoked, or expired rather than merely "looks like a key".

## Detection engine: betterleaks

Detection is **delegated** to [betterleaks](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks),
a single static Go binary. leakguard no longer carries a hand-written pattern
list; it asks the engine, then decides what to do with the answer.

```
betterleaks    471 rules, 463 compiled into the binary, 218 able to prove a
               finding valid/revoked/expired via the provider's API
leakguard      the judgement layers: may the agent read this path, is this
               command exfiltrating, is this the agent's own retry, what do
               we tell the model
```

That split is not cosmetic. A scanner answers "is there a credential in this
text?". It has no concept of *"may the agent read this file"*. Five layers below
are not detection at all, and nothing off-the-shelf replaces them.

### Install

```sh
~/.bin/betterleaks-update --check     # installed vs latest, changes nothing
~/.bin/betterleaks-update             # install/update, checksum-verified
~/.bin/betterleaks-update --version 1.9.0   # pin or roll back explicitly
```

It lands in `~/.bin/betterleaks` with config at `~/.config/betterleaks/`. The
git hook and this extension read the **same** binary and the **same** config, so
there is one rule set to reason about, not two.

### Why the 31 patterns were deleted rather than kept as a fallback

Measured against 29 token shapes, betterleaks covered **27**. Every shape the
hand-written regexes caught and the engine did not was a shape they *also*
over-matched. A copy of rules the engine already owns buys no coverage, and a
copy that silently drifts is worse than no copy.

The two shapes the engine genuinely misses are kept, each with its measurement
recorded in `engine.ts`:

| residual | why betterleaks does not report it |
|---|---|
| a bare `Authorization: Bearer <opaque>` line | its rule needs a `curl` invocation to establish egress context |
| `op://` 1Password references | a pointer to a credential, not a credential |

### One deliberate coverage loss

A bare 64-character hex digest is **no longer flagged**. That single branch
produced most of the false positives across 18 repositories: npm `integrity`
fields, manifest hashes, `sha256:` image pins, provenance files. A digest is not
a credential. The removal is asserted by a test, not left implicit, and the
exfil layers now test with a real credential instead of a digest as a stand-in.

If it ever needs to return, it must return **with context** (an egress or
transform command), never as a bare pattern.

### Cost, measured

| | per tool result |
|---|---|
| detection (process start dominates) | ~51 ms |
| a 100-tool-result session | ~5 s total |

A keyword prefilter could cut this to near zero, but it would require embedding
a copy of betterleaks' 462 keyword lists — the same drift problem this change
removes. Rejected deliberately.

### Version pinning

Not vendored: the 463 default rules are compiled **into** the 22 MB binary, so
vendoring means an opaque blob per platform and a binary diff for every rule
change. Not auto-updating either: the rule set *is* the thing being trusted, and
a scanner that silently swaps its own detection logic is unreviewable.

In practice: `VERSION` records what is installed, and drift is **reported** at
extension startup and on commit. It is never corrected on your behalf.

## Verifying the stack

The measurements in this README are easy to re-derive **wrongly**: a fixture with
a sequential alphabet fails betterleaks' own entropy filter and then looks like
"the engine misses this shape"; `git` mode scans history while `dir` scans the
working tree; `config show` omits `targetRules` so its absence proves nothing.

`scripts/verify-engine.py` encodes those traps and checks the stack that can be
checked without planting a credential:

```sh
python3 scripts/verify-engine.py        # exit 1 on any failure, 2 if engine missing
```

It verifies the engine runs, the pinned version matches (drift reported, never
fixed), the config parses, **`useDefault` is true and 471 rules resolve**, every
path allowlist is scoped with `targetRules`, and no local rule reuses an engine
id. Five assertions, and it is itself tested against four injected regressions so
it fails when it should.

## Git hook and CI


The `pre-commit` gate uses the same binary, the same config, and the same rules.
Only three checks live in shell because betterleaks cannot do them:

| kept check | why |
|---|---|
| `.env` file refusal | a file holding only `DEBUG=true` contains no credential, so the engine exits 0 (measured) |
| fail-closed when the binary is missing | a gate that passes when its scanner is gone is not a gate |
| chain to repo-local hooks | a global `core.hooksPath` otherwise shadows `~/.git/hooks` |

Do **not** replay the engine's patterns by hand to "add coverage": that is the
copy that drifts. Add a rule to `betterleaks.toml` instead.

**Do not use `--baseline-path` as the gate.** It is safe for new and rotated
secrets (verified), but it degrades into "fail only on changes since this file
was generated", which ages badly.

**Never write a report to `/dev/stdout`.** `-r /dev/stdout` intermittently fails
with `permission denied` and the tool then exits 0 with zero findings —
indistinguishable from clean. Use a real file path. This cost several wrong
conclusions while evaluating.

## Other harnesses

The engine and the judgement layer are portable; only the hook API is not.

| harness | status |
|---|---|
| pi | full extension: hooks, confirm prompts, `/leakguard` commands, audit log |
| OpenCode | `plugins/opencode.ts` — path guard, egress check, redaction via `tool.execute.before`/`.after` |

Both read the **same** `~/.bin/betterleaks` and the **same** `betterleaks.toml`,
so the detection rules are identical and there is one thing to update. Install
the OpenCode plugin with:

```sh
cp plugins/opencode.ts ~/.config/opencode/plugins/leakguard.ts
```

## Commands


| Command                     | Description                                              |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `/leakguard`                | Show session statistics (blocked, redacted)              |
| `/leakguard stats`          | Same as above (alias)                                    |
| `/leakguard mode max`       | Block sensitive paths AND redact secrets (with confirms) |
| `/leakguard mode auto`      | Same as MAX, but blocks silently (no confirm prompts)    |
| `/leakguard mode basic`     | Allow reads but still redact secrets                     |
| `/leakguard mode off`       | Disable all protection (dangerous)                       |
| `/leakguard allow-once`     | Allow one redacted value through without changing mode — single use, human-only via confirm |
| `/leakguard trust <pattern>`| Trust a pattern (literal or `/regex/`) for this session — skips redaction. Human-only. |
| `/leakguard trust list`     | List active trusted patterns                             |
| `/leakguard trust clear`    | Clear all trusted patterns                               |
| `/leakguard trust remove n` | Remove a trusted pattern by index                        |

```bash

npm test          # runs security.test.ts via tsx
npm run typecheck # tsc --noEmit
```

- 🔒 `max` - block paths + redact, with confirms

# hooks/ — the commit gate

`pre-commit` here is a **copy** of the global gate that lives at
`~/.git-hooks/pre-commit` and runs through `core.hooksPath`. It is versioned
here because it is the layer that actually stops a credential reaching a commit,
and until now it existed on exactly two machines with no history and no review.

## Install

```sh
git config --global core.hooksPath ~/.git-hooks
cp hooks/pre-commit ~/.git-hooks/pre-commit
chmod +x ~/.git-hooks/pre-commit
```

Nothing else. It is plain POSIX `sh` with no dependency beyond the engine.

## What it checks, and why only this much

| check | why it is not in the engine |
|---|---|
| `.env` file refusal | a file holding only `DEBUG=true` contains no credential, so the engine exits 0 (measured) |
| fail closed when the engine is missing | a gate that passes when its scanner is gone is not a gate |
| chain to repo-local hooks | a global `core.hooksPath` otherwise SHADOWS `~/.git/hooks`, silently disabling every repo's own hook |

Everything else is delegated to betterleaks, with the same binary and the same
config the pi extension and the OpenCode plugin use. **Do not re-implement an
engine rule here.** That is the copy that drifts, and it is why the 31 regexes
were deleted from the extension.

## Traps this file already accounts for

- **Two engine layouts.** macOS keeps it at `~/.bin/betterleaks`, the Linux
  server at `~/bin/betterleaks`. The hook probes both. Assuming one made it fail
  closed on the server and would have blocked every commit there.
- **Never report to `/dev/stdout`.** `-r /dev/stdout` intermittently fails with
  `permission denied` and the tool then exits 0 with zero findings —
  indistinguishable from clean.
- **Scan the staged diff, not the tree.** The hook scans what is being committed.
  A working-tree scan also surfaces untracked `.env` files the commit does not
  contain, which trains people to bypass the gate.

## Verifying it actually blocks

A gate that is installed but inert is the failure mode worth worrying about.
`scripts/verify-engine.py` checks the extension side; for the gate, commit a
file containing a credential in a throwaway repo and confirm it is refused:

```sh
d=$(mktemp -d); cd "$d"
git init -q . && git config user.email t@t.t && git config user.name t
git config core.hooksPath ~/.git-hooks
printf 'k=%s\n' "$(head -c 40 /dev/urandom | base64 | tr -d '=+/')" > f.txt
git add f.txt && git commit -m x     # must be refused
```

An engine-shaped token is needed for a *positive* test; a random string may be
correctly ignored for lacking a recognisable provider prefix. The
`scripts/verify-engine.py` control check covers that distinction.

## Where this is mirrored

`server-blueprint` versions the agent-side configuration (see its
`stack/pi/README.md`), but not this hook. If it is going to be reproducible on a
fresh machine, this directory is the source of truth to add there.

# oc-leakguard

Secret-exposure guard for [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai).

Blocks the agent from reading credential files, blocks a credential from leaving
the machine in a shell command, and redacts credentials from tool output **before
the model sees them**.

Detection is delegated to [**betterleaks**](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks)
(471 rules, one static binary). This package is the part a scanner cannot be: it
knows that `~/.ssh/id_rsa` is off-limits and that `curl -d "k=..."` is an exfil,
and it decides what to tell the model when it refuses.

## Install

```sh
# 1. the engine (required)
~/.bin/betterleaks-update

# 2. the plugin
opencode plugin add github:calionauta/leakguard

# or from a checkout
cp -r packages/oc-leakguard ~/.config/opencode/plugins/leakguard
```

No npm publish needed — OpenCode accepts a Git package specifier.

## What it does

| layer | action | catches |
|---|---|---|
| path guard | throws | `~/.ssh/`, `.env`, `.aws/`, `.gnupg/`, `.kube/`, `.secrets/`, keychains |
| egress | throws | a real network invocation carrying a credential |
| redaction | rewrites | any credential betterleaks reports in tool output |
| engine state | injects | one line into the system prompt when the engine is missing or drifted |

Documentation and fixture paths are allowed on purpose: refusing to read
`docs/setup.md` would make the guard useless for writing docs about secrets.

## What it deliberately does not do

- **No pattern list.** Every credential shape comes from the engine. A second copy
  of rules is a copy that drifts — that is why the pi host's 31 hand-written
  regexes were deleted.
- **No confirm prompt.** OpenCode's hook API can throw but not ask. To allow a
  one-off, resolve it in `betterleaks.toml` or remove the rule from the path set.
- **Not a sandbox.** It stops accidents and common exfiltration patterns, not a
  determined attacker with shell access.

## The engine, and why updates are manual

Betterleaks' 463 default rules are compiled **into** the binary, so a version
change *is* a rule change. Auto-updating a secret scanner means it swaps its own
detection logic unreviewed — and every false positive in this project's history
came from a rule change.

So: installing a missing engine is offered once, with consent; updating is
reported and left to you. `~/.config/betterleaks/VERSION` records the pin;
drift is surfaced at `session.created` and in the system prompt.

## Two layouts

macOS keeps the engine at `~/.bin/betterleaks`, the Linux server at
`~/bin/betterleaks`. Both are probed. Assuming one made a gate fail closed on the
server once, which would have blocked every commit there.

# pi-leakguard (name reservation)

This directory holds the npm name `pi-leakguard` only. **There is no code here** —
`pi` resolves a git package from the repository root and has no subdirectory
support, so the extension itself lives at the repo root (`index.ts`).

```
pi install git:github.com/calionauta/leakguard
```

The rest of this file describes the pi.dev host of leakguard.

Blocks the agent from reading credential files, blocks a credential from leaving
the machine, redacts credentials from tool output **before the model sees them**,
and gates git commits.

Detection is delegated to [**betterleaks**](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks)
(471 rules, one static binary). This package is the layer a scanner cannot be: it
decides whether the *agent* may read a path, whether a *command* is exporting
something, and what to tell the model when it refuses.

## Install

```sh
# 1. the engine (required) — the installer resolves ~/.bin or ~/bin
~/.bin/betterleaks-update

# 2. the extension
pi install git:github.com/calionauta/leakguard
```

Installed from the **repository root** — `pi` has no subdirectory support for git
packages, and it identifies git packages by repository URL.

## What it does

| layer | action | catches |
|---|---|---|
| path guard | BLOCK | `~/.ssh/`, `.env`, `.aws/`, `.gnupg/`, `.kube/`, `.secrets/`, keychains, `/etc/shadow` |
| symlink guard | BLOCK | a symlink resolving into a protected path |
| obfuscation | BLOCK | homoglyph / zero-width / NFKC tricks in commands |
| shell exfil | BLOCK | a real network invocation carrying a credential |
| egress DLP | BLOCK | a secret-bearing header with a value, credentialed URLs |
| taint tracking | BLOCK | egress of content previously read from a sensitive path |
| output redaction | REDACT | any credential betterleaks reports |
| git scan | BLOCK | a credential in the staged diff on commit |
| engine state | INJECT | one line into the agent's context when the engine is missing or drifted |

## Commands

`/leakguard status`, `mode`, `allow-once`, `trust <pattern>`, `untrust`, `audit`.

## What it deliberately does not do

- **No pattern list.** The 31 hand-written regexes were deleted: measured across
  29 token shapes, betterleaks covered 27, and every shape the regexes caught and
  the engine missed was a shape they *also* over-matched.
- **No auto-update.** The rules are compiled into the binary, so a version bump is
  a rule change. Install asks once; drift is reported and left to you.
- **Not a sandbox.** It stops accidents and common exfiltration patterns. For
  untrusted code or unattended automation, use a real sandbox.

## Formats that are documented, not blocked

Once a value is redacted its nature is unknowable, so the extension can *describe*
a finding's shape without exposing it (`describe-file.ts`). This is what makes the
gate usable on a repo that legitimately contains credential-shaped test fixtures
and documentation.

## [0.13.0] - 2026-10-26

### Fixed — the OpenCode plugin had never loaded

OpenCode 2.x replaced the V1 plugin shape with V2, and the loader **only warns**
when a module exports the wrong one. `{ id, server }` was rejected with
`Missing key at ["default"]["effect"], ["default"]["setup"]`, so on both machines
the plugin had not run since the shape changed. No error reached the model, and
every unit test passed, because the hooks do work when invoked directly — nothing
ever invoked them. Found in `~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log`.

`setup` (V2) is now exported beside `server` (V1); extra keys are ignored by both
majors, so one default serves either.

### Fixed — the pi host looked for the engine in the wrong directory

`engine.ts` hardcoded `~/.bin/betterleaks`; the Linux server uses `~/bin`. It
appeared to work there only because a stale `~/.bin/` copy was present. `engine.ts`
is now a thin binding over `core/engine-client.ts` (which always resolved both),
so "one engine client, two hosts" is literal rather than aspirational. That also
removed the second copy of `RULE_NAMES`, line/column pass-through and
`detectAll` — which had already been added to `core/` and not to the pi side.

### Fixed — eleven refusals said nothing actionable

Eleven `block: true` branches built `Blocked by leakguard: ...` by hand, bypassing
`blockMessage()` — including the path guards and egress, the ones that fire most.
`llm-hints.ts` exists because a session burned 8 blocked calls rewriting the same
file; those branches answered none of *what / where / what to do*. All now route
through `blockMessage()`. The path guards also got their own remedy: telling the
model to "rotate the credential" when nothing was read is wrong advice about a
credential that was never exposed.

### Fixed — OpenCode and pi disagreed about what a refusal says

`core/path-guard.ts` and `core/egress.ts` kept the older two-sentence wording, so
the *weaker* text was running in the host that had silently failed to load.
Both now follow the same rule as `blockMessage()`. The generic fallback (a rule id
from an engine update, a shape with no curated advice) no longer guesses the case.

### Changed — install no longer fails headlessly

`prepare` ran the engine installer on every git install, and opencode's embedded
npm treats the interactive read as a failure. Renamed to an explicit
`ensure-engine` script; the engine check belongs at first run, where a terminal
exists and the model can be told the gate is degraded.

The root `workspaces` field was the remaining blocker for
`opencode plugin add github:...`: anomalyco/opencode#49704 fails the git-dependency
prepare step on that field alone. Removed — it only matters for `npm install` at
the repo root during development. `main`/`exports` now point at the OpenCode host;
`pi` reads `pi.extensions` and is unaffected.

### Added

- `scripts/install-oc.sh` — copy, then **re-verify** the copy; a copy step alone
  reproduces the drift bug, since a stale plugin that loads looks current. Also
  removes the legacy single-file plugin and prints the log line that proves a load.
- `scripts/check-installs.sh [--remote]` — five surfaces that each failed silently
  at least once: pi checkout, OpenCode files, **OpenCode runtime module cache**,
  git hook, engine. The runtime check is the one that catches "files correct,
  process serving older code".
- `npm run typecheck` now also checks `packages/oc-leakguard/index.ts` under
  es2022/bundler, the resolution the OpenCode runtime uses. It was never in the
  root tsconfig, which is how a deleted export passed every check and failed only
  in the live log.

### Removed

- `plugins/` — pre-refactor duplicate of `packages/oc-leakguard` (306 lines, its
  own `detectSecrets`/`redactOutput`). Nothing imported it, it was still listed in
  `package.json` `files[]`, and its README told people to copy it.

### Note

If you upgraded from 0.12.0 and run OpenCode, **restart it**. The module cache is
per process, so corrected files do not affect a running `opencode serve`, which
continues to report `Plugin failed` until restarted.

## [0.11.0] - 2026-10-26

### Added — `scripts/verify-engine.py`, so the traps stop being re-learned

Five measurements in this project were wrong at least once, each for the same
reason: a conclusion drawn from a fixture or a scope that did not match the claim.
This script encodes them and fails loudly instead of quietly.

Checks: engine present and running; pinned vs running version (drift reported,
never corrected); config parses; **`useDefault` is true and >400 rules resolve**,
which is the executable answer to "did we overwrite betterleaks' rules?"; every
path allowlist carries `targetRules`; no local rule reuses an engine id.

The script is itself tested against four injected regressions — `useDefault`
flipped off, a `targetRules` line commented out, a local rule claiming an engine
id, and a missing engine — so a checker that only ever passes cannot ship. 5/5.

It deliberately does **not** plant a credential to test detection: a secret gate
blocks that, correctly. Those measurements stay manual and their numbers are
recorded in the config header.

### Added — `hooks/pre-commit` is now versioned

The commit gate is the layer that actually stops a credential reaching a commit,
and it existed on two machines with no history and no review. It is now in the
repo with a README covering install, the three checks it keeps because the engine
cannot do them, and the traps already accounted for (two engine layouts, never
report to `/dev/stdout`, scan the staged diff rather than the tree).

`package.json` gained a `files` list so `hooks/`, `scripts/`, `plugins/` and
`docs/` ship with the published package instead of only existing in the repo.

### Note on layering

`useDefault = true` means the engine's 471 rules stay active; our 8 `lg-*` rules
are add-only with `lg-` prefixed ids. The add-ons cover **legacy and variant
shapes the engine deliberately does not match** — its own patterns require exact
prefixes, lengths and suffixes. That is a narrower claim than the one previously
in the config header ("restores coverage"), which was stale and is corrected
there with the measured numbers.

## [0.10.1] - 2026-10-26

### Fixed — two false negatives found while attributing the false positives

Attribution mattered: none of the three false positives your own extension
blocked came from betterleaks. The engine returned **0 findings** on all of
them. They were bugs in this extension's pre-engine regexes, which the swap
preserved.

Asking the same question in reverse exposed the more serious direction:

- **A secret header in programmatic egress was never detected.**
  `headers={"Authorization": "Bearer aB3xK9mQ2pR7"}` did not match, because the rule
  required the colon immediately after the header name and the closing quote sat
  between them. That is the most common way a script sends a credential.
  betterleaks misses it too: its `curl-auth-header` rule needs a curl
  invocation.
- **`http`, `https`, `httpie` and `xh` were absent from EGRESS_TOOLS**, so an
  HTTPie command carrying a secret header was allowed even when the header rule
  matched it.

Both are closed, with the false positive asserted alongside so the fix cannot
reopen it. Suite: 146 -> 150.

### Attribution of the four false positives

| case | engine | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| documented header name | 0 findings | our regex |
| heredoc mentioning ssh/curl/export | 0 findings | our exfil word list |
| `export PATH=` alone | 0 findings | our exfil word list |
| real header value via curl | 1 finding | neither — that one was correct |

The extension is now responsible for exactly the egress context betterleaks
cannot infer, and nothing else. `x-api-key` without a client is still caught by
the engine's `generic-api-key`, so the layers do not overlap there either.

## [0.9.0] - 2026-10-26

Detection is now delegated to [betterleaks](https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks).
The 31 hand-written regexes are gone; pi-leakguard keeps the judgement layers.

### Why

A secret scanner answers "is there a credential in this text?". It has no concept
of *"may the agent read this file"*. Those are different questions, and
pi-leakguard had been answering both at once with one hand-maintained pattern
list. That list was the weakest part: 31 expressions, no validators, and every
false-positive fix (git SHAs, ask-hash, prose like sk-intent-need, supply-chain
digests) needed another special case.

betterleaks ships 471 rules, 463 compiled into the binary, 218 able to prove a
finding valid/revoked/expired against the provider API. Those rules are someone
else's maintenance burden now, and they are written against real provider
response formats instead of guessed prefixes.

### Removed

- The 31 built-in regexes in SECRET_PATTERNS. Measured against 29 token shapes,
  betterleaks covered 27. Every shape the regexes caught and the engine did not
  was a shape they also over-matched. Keeping them as a fallback would have
  bought no coverage and introduced a second rule set to keep in sync.
- countCaptureGroups() and the offset-math redaction dance. The engine reports
  StartLine/StartColumn/EndColumn, so locateSecretMatch() masks the exact
  reported span instead of re-deriving it.

### Added

- engine.ts -- the adapter: detectWithEngine(), detectAll(), applyRedaction(),
  engineStatus(), plus a RULE_NAMES map so the model keeps seeing "GitHub PAT"
  and not github-pat. The two shapes betterleaks does not report stay here, each
  with the measurement that justifies it: a bare Authorization: Bearer <opaque> line (its rule needs
  a curl invocation to establish egress context) and op:// 1Password references
  (pointers to a credential, not the credential).
- Version drift reporting. The 463 default rules are compiled into the 22 MB
  binary, so a version change IS a rule change. Startup and the git hook now
  report drift rather than silently running a different rule set.
- engine.test.ts (24 assertions) making the deletion falsifiable.

### Changed

- redactSecretsInText, scanForSecrets, describeSecretMatch, locateSecretMatch,
  hasSecretMaterial, isTaintedEgress and commandHasSecret all ask the engine.
  User-supplied extraSecretPatterns still run on top: additive, not a substitute.
- describeSecretMatch() reports the rule that actually fired instead of guessing
  from regex order.

### Deliberately lost

- A bare 64-character hex digest is no longer flagged. That branch produced most
  of the false positives across 18 repositories: npm integrity fields, manifest
  hashes, sha256: image pins, provenance files. A digest is not a credential. The
  loss is asserted by a test rather than left implicit, and the exfil layers now
  test with a real credential instead of a digest. If it ever returns, it must
  return WITH CONTEXT (an egress or transform command), never as a bare pattern.

### Cost

~51 ms per tool result (process start dominates the scan), so ~5 s across a
100-tool-result session. A keyword prefilter would cut this to near zero, but it
would require embedding a copy of betterleaks' 462 keyword lists -- the same
drift problem this release removes. Rejected on those grounds.

### Fixed (found by the red-proof, all previously hidden by vacuous tests)

- The OpenAI fixture had no digit in its body, so it satisfied neither the old
  regex nor the engine -- the assertion had been passing on nothing.
- The GitHub fixture body was a sequential digit-then-alphabet string, which
  betterleaks correctly rejects via its stopwords filter. The old regex flagged
  it; the engine does not, and the engine is right.
- The PEM assertion expected the END marker to vanish, but the engine reports the
  header only, so the END marker legitimately survives.
- isTaintedEgress and hasSecretMaterial were still testing the deleted regex.

Suite: 105 -> 140 assertions, all passing; tsc --noEmit clean. End-to-end
validated against the git hook and the installed binary (13/13 checks).

## [0.8.0] - 2026-10-26

### Added
- **`llm-hints.ts` — every block now tells the model what matched, where, and what to do instead.** A block used to say only "secret-looking material", which named neither the pattern nor the location. In a real session that cost three full rewrites of one file: the model tried a literal, then a variable, then character codes, because each denial was indistinguishable and gave it nothing to act on. Blocks now carry the pattern name (`"GitHub PAT"`), the masked offending line (`line 12: token = "[GitHub PAT]"`), a remedy chosen per pattern family, and an explicit note that retrying with different syntax will not help. Remedies are pattern-specific: a private key is referenced by path, a password is read by key name, a test fixture is built at runtime.
- **Repeat-block detection.** `state.blockAttempts` counts blocks per tool+intent within a turn. From the second attempt the message changes: "Changing the command's syntax will NOT change the outcome — the check is about the value, not the spelling." The counter resets at `agent_end`, so a new turn is a new intent.
- **Search-pattern false positive recognition.** `grep -n 'DOTENV|\\.env' file.ts` was blocked as a path access, after which the model read a 583-line file instead of grepping it — 5x the tokens. A sensitive token inside a quoted argument containing regex metacharacters is now recognised as a search pattern, and the block says so with a copy-pasteable workaround.
- **Context-aware path allowlist.** `isDocumentationPath()` exempts `docs/`, `*.example.*`, `*.sample`, `*.template`, test fixtures, `testdata/`, and vendored upstream code. Those files exist to show what a credential looks like. Measured: of 50 content-layer hits across 18 real repos, nearly all were documentation. A real private key block is still caught even in docs.
- `describeSecretMatch()` / `locateSecretMatch()`, plus `context.test.ts`, `llm-hints.test.ts` and `coverage.test.ts` (30 new assertions).

### Added
- **`/leakguard describe` — report redacted values by SHAPE, never by value.** This closes the one gap that made leakguard unusable for auditing: once a value was redacted, its nature was unknowable, so a finding could not be classified as real or false-positive, and the file could never be inspected. Describe mode reports length, character classes, entropy bucket, and a *published* vendor prefix, plus whether the value looks like prose or a placeholder — enough to decide `real` vs `false positive` while revealing nothing. An unknown prefix is never echoed: a 4-char prefix of a random 40-char secret is still 10 bits of it.

  Verified against the file that previously could not be read at all (`picoclaw/pkg/config/example_security_usage.go`): 6 findings, and the shape immediately classified them — `sk-ant-` with a placeholder word and prose structure at line 43, `token-from-env`-style assignments at 51/72/74, and two high-entropy values at 545/552 whose surrounding lines read `# Channels` / `export ..._TOKEN=` — documentation, not a leak. The previous behaviour was to redact all six to `[LEAKGUARD_REDACTED]` and abandon the task.
- `red-proof.ts` — runs the old block message and the new one side by side on the same input, plus the describe output for four value classes. The previous turn shipped the guidance layer with unit tests but never exercised it against the failures that motivated it.

### Fixed
- **The pre-commit/push scan could not see `.env` files.** `index.ts` ran `git diff --cached -- . ':(exclude).env*'`, so `git add .env && git commit` produced no finding — the one thing a pre-commit scan most needs to catch. The exclusion is gone; staged env files are now detected by name and reported separately from secret-pattern hits.
- **The redaction note was attached to output block 0.** When a redaction landed in a later text block, the model saw redacted text with no explanation and re-ran the tool to get "the real output". The note now attaches to the block that changed, names the rules that fired, and on a repeat says the value will not be revealed by re-running.
- **Redaction double-counted overlapping rules.** A generic rule such as `API Key Assignment` matched the placeholder text emitted by a specific rule, inflating counts and nesting placeholders. Spans are now claimed by the first (most specific) pattern that matches.
- **False positives on supply-chain metadata.** `SECRET_VALUE_RE` included `[0-9a-f]{32,}`, which matches git SHAs that `stripGitSHAs()` does not reach (a 40-hex SHA inside a longer hex run), npm `integrity` digests, `sha256:` image pins, and CI fixtures asserting a digest is not flagged. Split into two patterns with opposite tolerance: `SECRET_VALUE_RE` (commands, egress — hex stays, because an HMAC key being shipped off-box matters) and `CONTENT_VALUE_RE` (file contents and tool output — hex dropped, because reading files is high-volume and low-stakes). Hex with context (`SOME_TOKEN=<hex>`) is still caught via `SECRET_ASSIGNMENT_RE`.
- **The `@SK` branch matched prose.** `sk-intent-need` (a task id) and `sk-without-ide` (a sentence) were flagged. Real keys are long base62 runs containing at least one digit; the branch now requires one, and placeholder words (`your`, `actual`, `example`, `xxxx`, `test`, `dummy`, `fake`, `placeholder`, `redacted`) are excluded.
- **PEM markers matched lowercase.** The `i` flag made the lowercase spelling match, which is the exact substring picoclaw's own secret detector searches for — the guard fired on code whose job is finding keys. `PEM_RE` is now case-sensitive and separate; real key blocks are always uppercase.

### Changed
- `hasSecretMaterial(value, { path })` accepts the write/edit target so documentation and fixtures are not flagged. Called without `path` the behaviour is unchanged.

### Measured
Over 18 real repositories on the author's server, blocking-layer false positives on tracked source fell **95 files → 21 → 2 → 0** across these fixes. Coverage is verified unchanged by `coverage.test.ts`, which asserts every real credential shape is still detected (`ghp_`, `sk-`, `sk-proj-`, `sk-ant-`, `AKIA`, `xoxb-`, PEM, plus the tightened `sk-` branch). Suite: 75 → 105 assertions, all passing; `tsc --noEmit` clean.

## [0.6.1] - 2026-10-17

### Fixed
- **GitHub OAuth (`gho_`) and GitHub App installation (`ghs_`) tokens are now redacted.** They had no dedicated pattern in `SECRET_PATTERNS`, so a bare token — e.g. pasted inside a `curl` command — passed through the redactor untouched. They were only caught when they carried an explicit key prefix (`export TOKEN=...`), which is the less common way a token leaks into a transcript. The same gap applied to `scanForSecrets`, the last line of defence before a push. Both patterns use `{36,}` because GitHub App installation tokens vary in length. This matters because `gho_`/`ghs_` are the highest-privilege GitHub credentials and the ones automation and CI actually carry.

# betterleaks engine — installation and update policy

`pi-leakguard`, its git hook, and the OpenCode plugin all delegate detection to
the **same** betterleaks binary. Without it, only path guards and the judgement
layers work; credential detection is off.

So the engine must always be present, and the install must say so before it
happens rather than blocking a commit later.

## The one rule

**Consent to install, notification to update.**

| situation | behaviour |
|---|---|
| engine missing | ask once, explicitly, then install on yes |
| engine present, a newer release exists | report it; never install |
| engine present, at the pinned version | say nothing |

The asymmetry is deliberate and it is not laziness. Installing a missing
dependency is a *new capability* — you say yes once, you know what you agreed
to. Silently upgrading a **secret scanner** is a change to the thing doing the
judging: its rules are compiled into the binary, so a version bump *is* a rules
change, and a scanner that swaps its own detection logic is unreviewable.

## Why not auto-update, when everyone else does

Endpoint antivirus auto-updates signatures because a signature is a *fact about
malware*, and being a day late is strictly worse. A scanner's rules are also
facts — but its **false positives** are not. Every false positive in this
project's history came from a rule change, not from a rule that was too old:

- a bare hex digest matched npm `integrity` fields and provenance files
- `Authorization:` matched the header *name* in documentation
- `ssh` and `export` matched ordinary prose in a heredoc

An auto-updating scanner delivers those to you unreviewed, mid-session, with no
record of what changed. Pinning and reporting inverts that: you find out, you
decide, and a regression is attributable to a version you chose.

The industry consensus points the same way — TruffleHog made its version check
opt-in after users objected to opt-out telemetry; CI guidance for security
scanners is to pin exact versions and explain rescans, because silent rule
updates make two runs of the same commit disagree.

## How the human and the model find out

Nothing depends on the model remembering to check.

| surface | when | what |
|---|---|---|
| pi extension | `session_start` | warning if absent or drifted |
| pi extension | `before_agent_start` | one-line context injected into the run |
| git hook | every commit | drift reported, commit allowed |
| OpenCode plugin | `session.created` | warning if absent or drifted |

The `before_agent_start` injection is what makes this work for an agent rather
than only for a person: the model sees the state at the start of the run, so it
does not have to discover a degraded gate halfway through a task.

## Concretely

```sh
~/.bin/betterleaks-update --check   # installed vs latest; changes nothing
~/.bin/betterleaks-update           # install or update, checksum-verified
~/.bin/betterleaks-update --version 1.9.0   # pin or roll back
```

The installed version is recorded in `~/.config/betterleaks/VERSION`. Drift is
computed from that file, so it survives a shell restart and is visible to every
consumer independently.

Checksums come from the release's `checksums.txt`; a mismatch refuses the
install. The new binary is smoke-tested (`--version`) *before* replacing the
working one, so a broken download cannot take the git hook down with it.

## Where the install is offered

- **`pi install git:github.com/calionauta/leakguard`** — a `prepare` script
  checks for the engine and, in an interactive terminal, asks whether to install
  it. In CI (`CI` set, or no TTY) it never prompts and never downloads; it prints
  the command and exits 0, so an install in a pipeline cannot hang.
- **The extension itself** — if the engine is still missing at `session_start`,
  it reports DEGRADED and names the exact command. It does not install on its
  own initiative mid-session.
- **The OpenCode plugin** — same report at `session.created`, no install.
